justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a gently upward-sloping trajectory from roughly 311.5 at one day to 316 at one month. The one-day estimate is anchored almost entirely to the last observed price or index level, with only a small drift added to reflect the modest positive trend visible in recent data. By one week, I incorporate a slightly larger expected drift consistent with the underlying asset's historical tendency to grind higher in the absence of major catalysts, while acknowledging that mean-reversion forces keep the estimate from moving dramatically. At one month, the estimate continues that gradual climb, reflecting a longer window over which positive drift compounds, but the increment above the starting point remains modest because I do not have strong evidence of an imminent catalyst that would accelerate the move.

The width of the confidence intervals grows substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the natural accumulation of uncertainty over time. At one day, volatility is the dominant driver of interval width, and since daily price moves tend to be relatively contained, the band is fairly tight — about 19 points wide. By one week, I must account for several daily realizations of uncertainty stacking on top of each other, pushing the interval to roughly 36 points wide. At one month, a full range of macroeconomic surprises, earnings announcements, geopolitical developments, and liquidity shifts can materialize, widening the band to about 72 points. I also gave slightly fatter tails than a pure Gaussian model would suggest, because financial price distributions tend to exhibit excess kurtosis in practice.

There are several specific risks that could push realized outcomes outside even these wider bounds. On the downside, an abrupt deterioration in credit conditions, a surprise central bank policy shift toward aggressive tightening, or a geopolitical shock could cause sharp de-risking that breaks through the lower bound — particularly at the one-month horizon. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected macroeconomic release, a dovish policy pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push the level well above 352. Liquidity conditions also matter: if market depth deteriorates, even moderate order flow can produce outsized price swings that dwarf typical volatility estimates.

Finally, my intervals implicitly assume that the structural regime in place at the time of the forecast persists. If there is a regime change — for instance, a transition from low-volatility trending behavior to high-volatility mean-reverting behavior — then all three intervals would be too narrow and the point estimates could be systematically biased. Model uncertainty of this kind is difficult to quantify explicitly but represents perhaps the most serious tail risk for forecasts beyond a few days.
